newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish Peasants debate whether to keep coalition.
newsitem.headline: Polish Peasants debate whether to keep coalition.

text.p: Chiefs of Poland's Peasant party, stung by the sacking of one of its cabinet ministers, met on Friday to decide whether to stay in the ruling coalition with their larger ex-communist partner.

The Peasant party (PSL) leadership council gathered in Warsaw to discuss Wednesday's dismissal of Foreign Trade Minister Jacek Buchacz by Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz of the Democratic Left Alliance (SLD).
"If the prime minister and the SLD don't change the way they treat our party, the PSL cannot stay in the coalition," a Peasant leader, Aleksander Bentkowski, said before the meeting.
"There is also the question of passing through parliament the budget for next year, which is not acceptable in its current form," Bentkowski told reporters.
But President Aleksander Kwasniewski -- after meeting the PSL Senate speaker, Adam Struzik, -- played down the conflict, and said the coalition was likely to survive the current row.
"There is no crisis," Kwasniewski told a news briefing.
The SLD confirmed it wanted the coalition to stay in place until parliamentary elections, scheduled late last year.

"We aim at solving our country's problems quietly, within the current coalition, until the end of this parliament's term," SLD leader Jozef Oleksy told a news conference. He added the elections were likely to be held in October, 1997.

If the Peasants quit the coalition, the result may be a minority government of the SLD and spring parliamentary elections, which are otherwise not due until September 1997, sources close to Poland's presidential palace told Reuters.

The coalition has survived many rows, two sweeping cabinet reshuffles and growing policy differences between the two parties since the 1993 elections, when they beat parties rooted in the pre-1989 struggle against communist rule.

The firing of Buchacz, over what the government said was a blurring of private and public interests in granting of export guarantees, coincided with the parties rowing over cabinet posts during a reorganisation of ministries due this year.
Peasant leaders said they would demand an apology and set other conditions, apart from amendments to the budget draft.
Peasant parliamentarian Bogdan Pek said the party wanted to fill key economic ministries being created under the so-called centre reform, including a powerful new treasury ministry.
Pek also said his party would renew its demands to remove liberal SLD Privatisation Minister Wieslaw Kaczmarek, whom many PSL members accuse of selling off state firms too freely.
Senior SLD leader Leszek Miller said the row would not break the coalition and might help to sort out quarrels over posts under the reform, due to start next month. October 1.
SLD chiefs may call the PSL bluff, not least because an end to the coalition could serve their interests, analysts said.

The SLD has been leading in opinion polls, but its support has been slipping and a late August survey by the OBOP agency showed it running level at 21 percent with an opposition election alliance formed around the Solidarity union.

Early polls would allow it to campaign before the slide goes any further, while an SLD minority government, backed by the party's former leader, President Aleksander Kwasniewski, would be able to craft a 1997 budget aimed to win voters.
For this reason some PSL strategists, whose party now has only about 10 percent support, see the sacking of Buchacz as a provocation by the SLD to smash the alliance.
